units.text: INT. GHOSTS - CONTINUOUS
Impatiently.
Oh, do shut all the doors! This killing dread--
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Close the doors, Regina.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: REGINA shuts them and remains standing by the hall door.
MRS. ALVING takes her shawl off: REGINA does the same.
MRS. ALVING draws a chair across to OSWALD'S, and sits by him.
There now! I am going to sit beside you--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes, do. And Regina shall stay here too. Regina shall be with me always. You will come to the rescue, Regina, won't you?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: I don't understand--
units.name: REGINA

units.text: To the rescue?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes--when the need comes.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Oswald, have you not your mother to come to the rescue?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: You?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Smiles.
No, mother; that rescue you will never bring me.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Laughs sadly.
You! ha ha!
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Looks earnestly at her.
Though, after all, who ought to do it if not you?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Impetuously.
Why can't you say "thou" to me, Regina?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Note: "Sige du" = Fr. tutoyer.
Why don't you call me "Oswald"?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Softly.
I don't think Mrs. Alving would like it.
units.name: REGINA

units.text: You shall have leave to, presently. And meanwhile sit over here beside us.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: REGINA seats herself demurely and hesitatingly at the other side of the table.
And now, my poor suffering boy, I am going to take the burden off your mind--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: You, mother?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: --all the gnawing remorse and self-reproach you speak of.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: And you think you can do that?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes, now I can, Oswald. A little while ago you spoke of the joy of life; and at that word a new light burst for me over my life and everything connected with it.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Shakes his head.
I don't understand you.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: You ought to have known your father when he was a young lieutenant. He was brimming over with the joy of life!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes, I know he was.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: It was like a breezy day only to look at him. And what exuberant strength and vitality there was in him!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Well--?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Well then, child of joy as he was--for he was like a child in those days--he had to live at home here in a half-grown town, which had no joys to offer him--only dissipations. He had no object in life--only an official position. He had no work into which he could throw himself heart and soul; he had only business. He had not a single comrade that could realise what the joy of life meant--only loungers and boon-companions--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Mother--!
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: So the inevitable happened.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: The inevitable?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: You told me yourself, this evening, what would become of you if you stayed at home.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Do you mean to say that father--?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Your poor father found no outlet for the overpowering joy of life that was in him. And I brought no brightness into his home.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Not even you?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: They had taught me a great deal about duties and so forth, which I went on obstinately believing in. Everything was marked out into duties--into my duties, and his duties, and--I am afraid I made his home intolerable for your poor father, Oswald.
units.name: MRS. ALVING
